title: Welcome and Table of Contents
summary: What SS1 Biology First Term is about, how to use the notes, and a map of every unit.

p: Biology is the study of living things. It helps you to understand your own body, the plants and animals around you, the food we eat, diseases and how to avoid them, and how to look after the environment. It is a very important subject for medicine, farming, nursing, pharmacy and many other careers, and it is an examination subject in WAEC, NECO and JAMB.

In First Term you will learn how to recognise living things, how they are classified into groups, the structure and work of the cell, how substances move into and out of cells, nutrition, respiration, growth and how living things respond to their surroundings.

Read each unit slowly. Study the diagrams and, where you are asked, draw and label them in your notebook, because drawing is a main skill in Biology. At the end of every unit there are practice questions. They do not count towards a mark; they help you to check that you understood. Answer them all correctly to complete the unit.

title: Characteristics of Living Things
summary: What living things are and the ten characteristics that distinguish them from non-living things.

p: Everything in nature is either living or non-living. A living thing (organism) has life and shows certain characteristics that non-living things do not have. A stone does not feed, grow or reproduce; a goat does.

img.alt: A wheel diagram of the seven life processes: movement, respiration, sensitivity, growth, reproduction, excretion and nutrition, shown by the letters MRS GREN
img.cap: Seven life processes, remembered as MRS GREN (movement, respiration, sensitivity, growth, reproduction, excretion, nutrition).

p: 1. Movement: animals move from place to place, usually to find food. Plants move parts of their bodies in response to stimuli, for example shoots bending towards light.

2. Respiration: living things need energy for their activities. They get it by respiration, the release of energy from food. In aerobic respiration, food (glucose) is oxidised in the presence of oxygen to give energy, with carbon dioxide and water as by-products.
3. Nutrition: feeding. All organisms need food. Green plants make their own food (autotrophs). Animals depend on plants, directly or indirectly (heterotrophs).
4. Irritability (sensitivity): the ability to detect and respond to changes (stimuli) inside and outside the body, such as light, heat, water, sound and chemicals.
5. Growth: an irreversible increase in size, length and mass. It lets organisms repair and replace damaged or old tissues. The food eaten supplies what is needed for growth.
6. Excretion: removal of the toxic waste products of metabolism, such as carbon dioxide and urea, and of other unwanted substances.
7. Reproduction: producing offspring to continue the species. It can be sexual (two parents) or asexual (one parent).
8. Life span: each organism lives for a limited time and passes through birth, growth, maturity, decline and death.
9. Competition: living things compete for food, water, light, mates and space.
10. Adaptation: organisms have features that help them to survive in their environment, and they can adjust to change.
A crystal can grow by adding layers on its outside but it does not feed, respire or reproduce, so it is not living. Viruses are a special case; you will study them in Unit 5.

title: Plants and Animals Compared, and the Organisation of Life
summary: The main differences between plants and animals and the levels of organisation from cells to organ systems.

p: Most living things can be grouped as plants or animals. Study the table.

p: Life on Earth is organised in levels of increasing complexity. Cells are the basic structural and functional units of life, for example muscle cells and nerve cells. Tissues are groups of similar cells doing a particular job, for example muscle tissue contracts and nervous tissue carries signals. Organs are made of different tissues working together, for example the heart (cardiac muscle, blood vessels and connective tissue) pumps blood. Organ systems are groups of organs doing a complex job, for example the digestive system (stomach, liver, intestines). Above these come the whole organism, populations, communities and ecosystems, which you will study in Second Term.

title: Classification, Taxonomy and the Kingdoms
summary: Why we classify living things, Linnaeus and the seven taxonomic ranks, the binomial system of naming, and the five kingdoms.

p: Classification is grouping things according to their shared characteristics. In Biology it brings order to the huge variety of life. It makes living things easier to study, helps scientists talk about organisms clearly, and shows how organisms are related to one another (their evolutionary relationships).

Taxonomy is the science of classifying, naming and grouping organisms (from the Greek words for 'arrangement' and 'law'). The system used today is based on the work of the Swedish scientist Carolus Linnaeus. He arranged living things in seven major groups (ranks), from the largest to the smallest: Kingdom, Phylum (for animals) or Division (for plants), Class, Order, Family, Genus and Species. The basic unit of classification is the species: a group of organisms that can breed together and produce fertile offspring.

Linnaeus also introduced a way of naming organisms with two names. The first is the generic name (the genus) and begins with a capital letter. The second is the specific name (the species) and begins with a small letter. Scientific names are written in italics or underlined when written by hand. Examples: man, Homo sapiens; lion, Panthera leo; maize, Zea mays. (The source notes wrote 'panthera leo' and 'zea Mays', which break these rules.)

Linnaeus first divided living things into two kingdoms, plants and animals. But many one-celled organisms did not fit well. Biologists later divided living things into five kingdoms: Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae and Animalia (this five-kingdom system was proposed by R. H. Whittaker in 1969). Viruses do not fit into any of the five and are treated separately.

title: Viruses, and the Kingdoms Monera, Protista and Fungi
summary: Why viruses are special, and the features of the kingdoms Monera, Protista and Fungi with examples.

p: A virus is so small that it can be seen only with an electron microscope. It has either DNA or RNA inside a protein coat. It has no cell structure, cannot make its own proteins, and does not respire, feed or excrete. It cannot reproduce by cell division (binary fission); it reproduces only inside a living host cell.

Viruses are like living things because they reproduce inside a host cell and pass their characteristics to the next generation. They are like non-living things because outside a host they can form crystals and do not respire, excrete or respond to stimuli. So they are treated separately from the five kingdoms. Examples of diseases: the common cold, influenza, polio, measles, HIV and COVID-19.

These are the simplest living things: bacteria and blue-green bacteria (cyanobacteria, like Anabaena). They are microscopic and single-celled. They are prokaryotes: they have no true nucleus (no nuclear membrane), and the DNA lies in the cytoplasm. Their cell wall does not contain cellulose; it is made of peptidoglycan (a mixture of sugars and amino acids). (The source says 'protein and fatty materials'.) They have no organelles with membranes except ribosomes. They reproduce asexually by binary fission.

Protists are mostly single-celled eukaryotes: their cells have a definite nucleus. Most live in water. They move by cilia, flagella or pseudopodia. Some are free-living and a few are parasites. There are two groups: Protozoa, which are animal-like (Amoeba, Paramecium, Plasmodium, Trypanosoma), and Protophyta, which are plant-like (diatoms, Chlorella, Chlamydomonas). Euglena has both plant-like and animal-like features.

Fungi are non-green organisms without chlorophyll, so they cannot photosynthesise. They have rigid cell walls made of chitin and other polysaccharides. They have no true roots, stems or leaves. Most are non-motile. They reproduce by spores (asexual) and also sexually. Most are saprophytes (feeding on dead matter); some are parasites. A few are single-celled (yeast) but most are many-celled (Rhizopus, Mucor, mushrooms). They store food as glycogen.

title: Kingdom Plantae
summary: The main groups of plants: thallophytes, bryophytes and tracheophytes, and how seed plants divide into gymnosperms and angiosperms, monocots and dicots.

p: Plants are multicellular, non-motile organisms. Their cells have cellulose cell walls and chloroplasts containing chlorophyll, which lets them make food by photosynthesis. The kingdom is divided into three main groups: Thallophyta, Bryophyta and Tracheophyta.

img.alt: A flow chart of the plant kingdom: thallophytes, bryophytes and tracheophytes; tracheophytes divide into pteridophytes and spermatophytes; spermatophytes divide into gymnosperms and angiosperms; angiosperms divide into monocots and dicots

p: Example: algae. No true roots, stem or leaves. Chlorophyll is present.
Examples: mosses and liverworts. No true roots, stem or leaves; they have thread-like rhizoids that anchor them.

The tracheophytes have vascular tissue (xylem and phloem). They include two groups. Pteridophytes (ferns) have true roots, stems and leaves but reproduce by spores. Spermatophytes make pollen and seeds. They divide into gymnosperms (have cones and naked seeds, usually needle-like leaves, no flowers; for example pine) and angiosperms (flowering plants whose seeds develop inside fruits).

Angiosperms are divided into two classes. Monocots have one seed leaf (cotyledon), parallel-veined narrow leaves; there are no true trees except palms (examples: maize, grasses, palms). Dicots have two seed leaves, net-veined broad leaves; they include herbs, shrubs and trees (examples: beans, hibiscus, mango).

title: Kingdom Animalia (1): Invertebrates
summary: The main phyla of animals without backbones: Porifera, Cnidaria, Platyhelminthes, Nematoda, Annelida, Mollusca, Arthropoda and Echinodermata, with their features and examples.

p: The animal kingdom divides into invertebrates (no backbone) and vertebrates (with a backbone). Here are the main invertebrate phyla.

img.alt: A chart of animal classification: vertebrates (mammals, birds, reptiles, amphibians, fish) and invertebrates (Porifera, Cnidaria, Annelida, Mollusca, Platyhelminthes, Echinodermata, Arthropoda with Crustacea, Arachnida, Insects and Myriapoda)

p: Protozoa (single-celled; now usually classified with the protists): Amoeba, Plasmodium, Trypanosoma. Mostly microscopic. Some are free-living and some are parasites.

Porifera (sponges): many-celled, fixed in one place (sessile), mostly aquatic. One body cavity with many pores; two layers of cells; skeleton of calcium carbonate or silica spicules; no nervous system; reproduce asexually by budding.

Cnidaria / Coelenterata (Hydra, sea anemone, jellyfish): simple many-celled aquatic animals with two cell layers and no organs; stinging cells (nematoblasts); asexual reproduction by budding and sexual by gametes.

Platyhelminthes (flatworms): liver fluke, tapeworm, planaria. Flat, thin bodies, bilaterally symmetrical, three body layers, mostly hermaphrodites, free-living or parasitic; one opening to the gut (the mouth).

Nematoda (roundworms): Ascaris, hookworm, guinea worm, filaria worm, Onchocerca. Long, slender, cylindrical bodies with pointed ends; three layers; mouth and anus; covered with a cuticle; separate sexes; free-living or parasitic. (The source lists tapeworm here, but tapeworms are flatworms.)
Annelida (segmented worms): earthworm, leech (Hirudo), Lumbricus. Long, cylindrical, segmented bodies; three layers; mouth and anus; nervous, excretory, reproductive and circulatory systems.
Mollusca: snail, slug (also oyster and octopus). Soft unsegmented body usually covered by a calcareous shell; head, muscular foot and a visceral hump; eyes and tentacles on the head.
Echinodermata: starfish, sea urchin. Aquatic; radially symmetrical; spiny skin with a calcareous skeleton; tube feet for movement; separate sexes.

The biggest phylum. Arthropods have jointed legs, a hard exoskeleton of chitin and segmented bodies. There are four classes (the source notes wrongly list 'Annelida' as a fifth; Annelida is a separate phylum).

Class Insecta (cockroach, housefly, butterfly, grasshopper): a pair of antennae, a pair of compound eyes, body in head, thorax and abdomen, three pairs of legs on the thorax, breathing by tracheae, often winged, and they usually go through metamorphosis.

img.alt: A labelled grasshopper showing the head, thorax and abdomen, antenna, foreleg, midleg, hind leg, femur, tibia and forewing

p: Class Myriapoda (centipede and millipede): head and a long trunk of many segments; each segment of a centipede (class Chilopoda) has one pair of legs and the animal is a carnivore; each segment of a millipede (class Diplopoda) has two pairs of legs and it eats plants; breathing by tracheae.

Class Arachnida (spiders, scorpions, ticks): two body regions, the prosoma (cephalothorax) and the opisthosoma (abdomen); four pairs of walking legs; chelicerae and pedipalps; usually simple eyes; breathing by book lungs.

Class Crustacea (crab, prawn, shrimp, water flea, barnacle): two body regions, the cephalothorax and the abdomen; two pairs of antennae; usually five pairs of walking legs; compound eyes; gills for breathing; mostly aquatic.

title: Kingdom Animalia (2): Vertebrates
summary: The five classes of vertebrates (fishes, amphibians, reptiles, birds, mammals) with their features and examples.

p: Vertebrates have a backbone (vertebral column) and are divided into five classes: Pisces (fishes), Amphibia, Reptilia, Aves (birds) and Mammalia. (The source notes misspell 'Aves' as 'Eves'.)

Gills for breathing, which stay in the adult. Paired pectoral and pelvic fins. Lateral line for sensing movement. Skin with scales (cycloid scales in bony fishes such as tilapia, placoid scales in cartilaginous fishes such as dogfish). External fertilisation.

img.alt: A labelled fish showing dorsal fin, caudal fin, pectoral fin, pelvic fin, anal fin, mouth and gill flap
img.cap: A bony fish, with its fins labelled.

p: Pentadactyl limbs (five digits). Soft, moist skin without scales. Gills at the tadpole stage and lungs in the adult (also breathing through the skin). Eardrum on the surface, no external ear. External fertilisation in water. Examples: toad, frog, newt and salamander. (The source says 'strew', a mistake for 'newt'; shrews are mammals.)

img.alt: A frog and a toad with labels: bulging eye, tympanic membrane, trunk, forelimb, hind limb and webbed feet

p: Pentadactyl limbs. Dry skin covered with scales. Breathe with lungs. Eggs with a leathery shell and plenty of yolk, laid on land; no larval stage. Internal fertilisation. Examples: lizard, snake, crocodile, tortoise.

img.alt: A lizard with labels: head, nostril, bulging eye, ear drum, trunk, fore-limb, hind limb, tail, cloaca and clawed digits

p: Pentadactyl limb, with the forelimb changed into a wing. Warm-blooded. Feathers on the body and scales on the legs and feet. A beak and no teeth. Lungs for breathing. Hard-shelled eggs with much yolk. No larval stage. Internal fertilisation. Examples: pigeon, domestic fowl.

img.alt: A bird with labels: crown, head, nape, back, rump, tail, wing, breast, belly, thigh, leg, upper beak and lower beak

p: Pentadactyl limbs. Warm-blooded. Hair on the skin, and sweat glands. Mammary glands that produce milk for the young. A four-chambered heart. Internal fertilisation. Most are viviparous (the young develop inside the mother); a few, such as the platypus, lay eggs. Examples: man, goat, dog, bat, whale.

title: The Cell: Forms of Cells and the Plant and Animal Cell
summary: What a cell is, the forms in which cells exist, and the structure of typical plant and animal cells.

p: A cell is the basic structural and functional unit of all living things, the smallest unit of life that can carry out life processes. Cells differ in structure, function and size, but all have a cell membrane, genetic material (DNA or RNA) and the ability to carry out metabolism and reproduce.
1. Single (unicellular) cells: the whole organism is one cell. Examples: bacteria, Amoeba, Euglena, yeast.
2. Colonies: groups of cells living together, each able to live independently. Examples: Volvox, some algae and bacteria.
3. Filaments: cells joined end to end in a chain or thread. Examples: Spirogyra (a green alga), some cyanobacteria.
4. Part of a many-celled organism: cells organised into tissues, organs and systems, as in a plant or an animal.

A plant cell has a rigid cell wall of cellulose outside the cell membrane, chloroplasts, a large central vacuole, a nucleus, cytoplasm, mitochondria, endoplasmic reticulum, ribosomes and the Golgi apparatus.

img.alt: A labelled plant cell showing the cell wall, cell membrane, cytoplasm, nucleus, nucleolus, vacuole, chloroplast, mitochondria, ribosomes, endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi apparatus and amyloplast

p: An animal cell has a cell membrane but no cell wall, no chloroplasts and usually small vacuoles. It has a nucleus, cytoplasm, mitochondria, ribosomes, endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi body, lysosomes and centrioles.

img.alt: A labelled animal cell showing the plasma membrane, nucleus, chromatin, nuclear pores, rough and smooth endoplasmic reticulum, ribosomes, centriole, mitochondrion, Golgi body, lysosome and vacuole

title: Cell Organelles and Their Functions
summary: The functions of the cell membrane, nucleus, cytoplasm, mitochondria, ribosomes, endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi body, lysosomes, vacuoles and other organelles, and a plant-animal comparison table.

p: Cell membrane: controls what enters and leaves the cell; a protective barrier. Nucleus: contains the DNA and controls the cell's activities. Cytoplasm: a jelly-like fluid in which organelles are suspended and many reactions take place. Endoplasmic reticulum (ER): rough ER (with ribosomes) makes proteins; smooth ER makes lipids and helps remove poisons. Golgi apparatus: changes, packages and transports proteins and lipids. Mitochondria: the 'powerhouses', where cellular respiration releases energy. Ribosomes: make proteins using the instructions from DNA. Lysosomes: contain enzymes for digestion and for removing waste. Vacuole: stores nutrients and wastes; in plants it is large and keeps the cell firm (turgid). Chloroplast (plants): carries out photosynthesis. Cell wall (plants): gives shape and support. Cytoskeleton: gives support and helps movement. Centrioles (animal cells): help in cell division.

title: Diffusion
summary: What diffusion is, how it happens, the factors that affect its speed and why it is important to living things.

p: Diffusion is the spontaneous movement of particles (atoms, ions or molecules) from a region where they are in high concentration to a region where they are in low concentration. They move down a concentration gradient until they are evenly spread (equilibrium). The particles move by random motion, and no energy from the cell is needed. Diffusion happens in gases, liquids and, very slowly, solids. Examples: the scent of flowers spreading through a room; a drop of ink spreading in water; oxygen entering the blood in the lungs.

img.alt: Two panels: osmosis, with water crossing a semipermeable membrane from pure water to a solution; and diffusion, with red particles spreading from high concentration to low concentration

sections.h: Factors affecting the rate of diffusion
p: Temperature: higher temperature makes particles move faster, so diffusion is faster. Concentration gradient: a steeper gradient gives faster diffusion. Size of the particles: small particles diffuse faster than large ones. The medium: diffusion is fastest in gases, slower in liquids and slowest in solids. Surface area: a larger surface (such as the many folds of the gut) lets more diffuse. Distance: shorter distances give faster diffusion.

sections.h: Importance of diffusion to living things
p: 1. Gas exchange: oxygen and carbon dioxide diffuse in and out of the body in the lungs, leaves and gills.
2. Respiration and photosynthesis: gases move in and out of cells to supply these processes.
3. Uptake of nutrients: digested food diffuses across the gut wall into the blood, and wastes diffuse out of cells.
4. Mixing for chemical reactions: diffusion brings reactants together in the cell.
5. In plants, water vapour diffuses out of the leaves through the stomata (transpiration).

title: Osmosis and Active Transport
summary: Osmosis, tonicity (hypertonic, hypotonic and isotonic solutions), plasmolysis, turgidity, haemolysis, the importance of osmosis, and active transport.

p: Osmosis is the movement of water molecules from a region of lower solute concentration (a dilute solution, which has more free water) to a region of higher solute concentration (a concentrated solution, which has less free water) through a semi-permeable (selectively permeable) membrane. The membrane lets water through but not all dissolved substances. It happens only when a membrane separates a weak solution from a strong one. (It is easy to be confused by the wording: the 'concentration' referred to is the concentration of the dissolved substance.)

Hypertonic: the surrounding fluid is more concentrated than the cell contents. Water leaves the cell by exosmosis and the cell shrinks. Hypotonic: the surrounding fluid is less concentrated than the cell contents. Water enters the cell by endosmosis and the cell swells. Isotonic: the same concentration inside and out; there is no net movement of water.

Plant cell: in a hypotonic solution, it takes in water and becomes turgid (swollen and firm), which gives support. In a hypertonic solution, it loses water and becomes flaccid (limp); with severe loss, the cell membrane pulls away from the cell wall, which is called plasmolysis. Plasmolysis can be reversed (deplasmolysis) if the cell is placed in a hypotonic solution. Animal cell: a red blood cell in a hypotonic solution takes in water and may burst (haemolysis); in a hypertonic solution, it shrinks.

img.alt: A plant cell and a red blood cell shown in hypertonic, isotonic and hypotonic solutions: shrunken or plasmolysed, normal, and swollen (turgid or bursting)
img.cap: Plant and animal cells in hypertonic, isotonic and hypotonic solutions.

p: 1. It absorbs water from the soil into the root hairs. 2. It moves water from cell to cell in plants. 3. It controls opening and closing of the stomata (guard cells). 4. It makes plant cells turgid, which supports non-woody parts. 5. It moves water between cells in animals. 6. It reabsorbs water from the kidney tubules into the blood. 7. It can cause haemolysis of red blood cells if they are in pure water.

Osmoregulation is the control of the amount of water and dissolved substances in an organism, so that its internal environment stays balanced. It uses osmosis and active transport. For example, the kidney controls the water content of the blood.

Active transport is the movement of substances against a concentration gradient (from low to high concentration) using energy (ATP) from respiration. It needs carrier proteins in the cell membrane. Examples: root hairs absorbing mineral salts from soil that are in lower concentration than inside the cell; absorption of glucose from the gut.
